explanation:
## The whole counting loop

```cpp
std::map<std::string, int> count;

std::string word;
while (std::cin >> word)
{
    for (char& c : word)
        if (c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z') c = static_cast<char>(c - 'A' + 'a');
    ++count[word];
}
```

Four lines, and the interesting one is the last.

## What `count[word]` does when the key is new

```cpp
++count[word];
```

`operator[]` on a map **inserts** the key if it is absent, value-initialises the
value, and returns a reference to it. Value-initialising an `int` gives `0`, so
`++` makes it `1`. For a key already present it returns a reference to the
existing count, and `++` makes it one more.

So one expression handles both cases, and the "have I seen this word before"
question never has to be asked. Written out, the explicit version is:

```cpp
auto it = count.find(word);
if (it == count.end()) count.insert({ word, 1 });
else                   ++it->second;
```

Correct, five times longer, and does two lookups in the branch that inserts.

**The flip side, and it bites people:** `operator[]` inserts on *read* too.

```cpp
if (count["cache"] > 0) { ... }        // just inserted "cache" with value 0
```

Looking a key up this way creates it. If you only want to ask whether a key
exists, use `count.contains(word)` (C++20) or `count.find(word) != count.end()`.
And note that `operator[]` is therefore not available on a `const` map at all -
it cannot be, since it may modify the container.

## Why no sorting step

Iterating a `std::map` visits its keys in ascending order, because that is how it
stores them - a balanced binary search tree, ordered by `std::less` on the key.
So:

```cpp
for (const auto& entry : count)
    std::cout << entry.first << ' ' << entry.second << "\n";
```

prints alphabetically, with no `std::sort` anywhere. The container was chosen
because it already has the property the output format needs.

The alternative is `std::unordered_map`, a hash table: lookups are O(1) average
instead of O(log n), and iteration order is **unspecified** - it depends on the
hash function and the bucket count, and it can change between runs or library
versions. For this problem that would mean collecting the entries into a vector
and sorting them afterwards. Worth knowing both, and worth knowing which
question each answers:

| | `std::map` | `std::unordered_map` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| lookup | O(log n) | O(1) average |
| iteration order | sorted by key | unspecified |
| needs from the key | `<` | a hash and `==` |
| memory | node per element, pointer-chasing | buckets, better locality |

## `const auto&` in the loop

```cpp
for (const auto& entry : count)
```

Each element of a map is a `std::pair<const std::string, int>`, so `entry.first`
is the word and `entry.second` is the count. Writing that type out is noisy,
hence `auto`.

The `&` matters: without it each iteration **copies** the pair, including a heap
allocation for the string. The `const` says the loop only reads. Together they
are the default form for iterating any container of non-trivial elements.

C++17 can name the two halves directly, which reads better:

```cpp
for (const auto& [word, n] : count)
    std::cout << word << ' ' << n << "\n";
```

## The tie-break falls out of the order

```cpp
if (entry.second > bestCount) { bestCount = entry.second; best = entry.first; }
```

Strictly greater, not `>=`. Since the walk is alphabetical, the first word to
reach the maximum count is kept and no later word with the *same* count
displaces it - which is precisely "the alphabetically first of those tied".

Change it to `>=` and the **last** tied word wins instead. The hidden case
`z y z y x` is there for this: `y` and `z` both appear twice, the answer is `y`,
and `>=` reports `z`.

This is the useful observation. The tie-break was not implemented; it was
obtained by walking the data in the right order and comparing strictly. When a
tie-break happens to match the iteration order, that is the cheapest way to get
it - and when it does not, you need an explicit comparison, so it is worth
noticing which situation you are in.

## Lowercasing in place

```cpp
for (char& c : word)
```

`char&`, so the characters of `word` are modified rather than copies of them.
Without the `&` the loop runs, changes nothing, and every capitalised word is
counted separately - the same missing-ampersand failure as the clamp problem,
one container deeper.

## The empty input

`distinct 0`, no word lines, and `bestCount` still `0`, so `top none 0`. Reporting
an empty word with a count of zero would be worse than saying there is no answer -
and `top none 0` is a shape a caller can test, which is the point of defining it
rather than leaving it to whatever falls out.
